migrationNotes: Spine: follow one sealed envelope from 'nobody has looked' to a verdict, then flip the claim and end on a claim people dispute.
Each stop adds one idea (claim, truth value, negation), always tested against the envelope or a lamp.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): what-logic-operates-on-hook, what-logic-operates-on-verdict-check, what-logic-operates-on-negation-check.

lesson.title: What logic operates on

lead.text: Go back to the envelope. Mia's sentence, “It holds a £10 note”, says how things are. That makes it something anyone could check. Open the envelope and either she was right or she was wrong. A sentence like that is called a claim.

Not every sentence works this way. “Is there a note in the envelope?” asks for information. It can be answered, but it can't be right or wrong in the way Mia's sentence can. “Open the envelope” is a command, and a command can be obeyed or ignored without ever being wrong. Only a sentence that says how things are can turn out to be wrong.

That gives the first skill in logic, which is sorting. Faced with a sentence, ask whether it says how things are. If it does, it is a claim and there is something to test. If it asks or tells, it is a different kind of sentence and there is nothing to test.

diagram.alt: Six sentences sorted into three groups: two that say how things are, two questions and two commands.
diagram.caption: Sentences sorted by what they do. Only the ones that say how things are can turn out to be wrong.

lead.text: A lamp stands in a corner of the room. A sentence about it can say how it is, ask about it or tell someone what to do with it.

Back to Mia and Jon. Mia's claim is waiting for a verdict, and the verdict comes from checking the claim against how things are. If the envelope holds a £10 note, her claim passes. If it holds anything else, or nothing, her claim fails. That verdict is the claim's truth value, and the two values on offer are true and false.

Look at who sets the verdict. The envelope does. Nobody has opened it, but it still holds exactly what it holds, so Mia's claim already has a truth value. All that is missing is anyone knowing it. Calling a claim “unknown” describes what we have found out so far, and the claim itself already has one value. A third value never joins the list.

So in any real situation a claim has exactly one truth value, and that value is one of two. Jon's sentence, “It doesn't”, is the other side of the same envelope. Whichever way the envelope turns out, one of the two sentences passes and the other fails.

diagram.alt: An envelope shown sealed, then holding a ten pound note, then empty, with the verdict on Mia and Jon sentences under each.
diagram.caption: Pick what the envelope holds. Whichever it is, one sentence is true and the other false.

lead.text: Mia's claim is waiting for a verdict and nobody has looked. Think about which verdicts a claim can end up with, then count them.

reveal.text: Two: true and false. If you were tempted to count “unknown”, remember that the word describes what we know. The envelope still holds what it holds.

lead.text: Put Jon's sentence next to Mia's. Jon's sentence is Mia's claim with “not” put in, and it says that her claim fails. Logic has a name and a symbol for that move.

Writing out whole sentences gets tedious, so a claim is given a short name, usually the letter p. If p is “The lamp is on”, then ¬p is “The lamp is not on”. The symbol ¬ reads “not”, and ¬p is called the negation of p. It is a claim in its own right, so it has a truth value of its own.

The envelope shows how the two values are related. Mia's claim and Jon's are negations of each other, and they can't both pass or both fail. Whichever way the envelope is, one of them is right and the other wrong. That is what the next screen asks you to work out for the lamp.
Suppose p is “The lamp is on”, and the lamp is on.

reveal.text: The table shows both rows, and your answer matches the first one: negation turns each value into the other.

lead.text: A claim doesn't have to be easy to settle. The envelope can be opened in a moment, but some claims are hard to check and some are argued about for years. Two people can disagree sharply about whether a soup is too salty, and nobody calls the sentence “This soup is too salty” a question or a command.

What makes it a claim is that the speaker says how something is. Whether anyone can settle the matter, and whether anyone agrees, comes afterwards. The same holds for a claim about something hidden, such as a coin under a cup. A claim about something nobody has measured yet works the same way. Each is checked against how things are, and each has a truth value whether or not we can find it.

Logic does not decide matters of taste or fill in missing information. It starts from sentences that say how things are, and it asks what follows once their truth values are fixed. The last screen of the lesson tests the sorting on a sentence that people dispute.
Two friends argue about a painting. One says: “This painting is beautiful.” The other disagrees.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish truth-apt claims from questions and commands, including claims whose truth is unknown or disputed.
lesson.nextAction: A claim can be true or false, even when its truth is unknown.

blocks.text: Mia and Jon are arguing over a sealed envelope. Mia says: “It holds a £10 note.” Jon says: “It doesn't.” Nobody has opened it, so nobody can say who is right, and the argument goes round in circles for a while.

Anyone listening can tell something is odd about it. Mia and Jon are both talking about what is in the envelope, and the envelope isn't saying anything. It holds a note or it doesn't, and that was settled when someone sealed it. They are arguing about a fact that already exists and that neither of them knows.

Logic starts with sentences like theirs. First we sort out which sentences can be wrong at all. Then we look at what it means that nobody has looked yet, and at how to state the opposite of a sentence. The lesson ends with a sentence that people argue about even though there is nothing to open.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell claims from questions and commands, and know a claim has one truth value even when you can't see it.
intro.whyItMatters: Arguments are built from claims, so spotting one is the first step to testing an argument.

recap.keyIdea: Logic works on claims. In any situation a claim has exactly one truth value, whether or not anyone knows it. Negation reverses that value.

blocks.text: Back at the sealed envelope, you decided that it already holds what it holds, so Mia's claim already has an answer. You flipped a claim with negation and saw that a lamp that is on makes “the lamp is not on” false. You also saw that a claim people argue about, like “This painting is beautiful”, is still a claim.

recap.nextHook: Mia and Jon each made one claim. Sam makes a single promise with two parts joined by “if”, and the next lesson works out exactly when a promise like his is broken.

hints: Which sentence could someone check and find wrong?
Compare an assertion with a question and with an instruction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The lamp is on” says how things are, so it can be checked. A question asks and a command directs.

questions.onCorrect: The lamp either is on or isn't, so it can be checked. A question asks and a command directs; neither can be wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That asks for information. It says nothing about how things are, so nobody can find it wrong.
That tells someone to act. It can be obeyed or ignored, but not found wrong.

questions.prompt: In this course, how many different truth values can a claim have?
hints: Before the envelope is opened, which verdicts could Mia's claim get?
Is “unknown” a fact about the envelope, or about you?
List the verdicts the envelope itself could make Mia's claim have, then count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A claim is true or false in a case: two values.

questions.onCorrect: Two. “Unknown” describes what you know, not the claim: the envelope holds the note or it doesn't.

misconceptions.feedback: “Unknown” describes you, not the claim. The envelope already holds what it holds.
A claim can fail as well as hold. Think of Jon's claim when the note is there.

questions.prompt: When p is true, is ¬p true or false?
hints: ¬p says that p is not the case.
If the lamp is on, is “the lamp is not on” correct?
questions.onCorrect: False. ¬p makes the opposite claim, so it takes the opposite truth value.

misconceptions.feedback: ¬p says the lamp is not on. Does that match a lamp that is on?

questions.prompt: How should we treat “This painting is beautiful” here?
hints: The speaker is saying how the painting is, even if others disagree.
Does the sentence ask for anything, or tell anyone to do anything?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It asserts an evaluation, so it is a claim, though people dispute it.

questions.onCorrect: It asserts an evaluation, so it is a claim. Disagreement doesn't turn a claim into a question or command.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody is told to do anything. The speaker says how the painting is.
It asks for nothing. It states a view, which others may dispute.

questions.prompt: Is “Close the window” a claim or a command? Use one word.
hints: Ask whether the sentence says how things are or directs someone to act.
The verb “Close” asks for an action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It directs an action rather than asserting a truth.

questions.onCorrect: Command. It directs an action; it doesn't say how anything is, so it can't be true or false.

misconceptions.feedback: Could anyone find “Close the window” wrong? It tells someone what to do.

questions.prompt: A claim is false. Is its negation true or false?
hints: Apply negation to the false claim.
Negation never leaves the value alone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation of a false claim is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. Negation reverses the value, so the negation of a false claim is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Negation never leaves the value alone. Ask what ¬ does to a claim.

hints: Could the envelope hold a £10 note and not hold one?
Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. Does it change what is inside?

acceptedIdeas: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exactly one of them. The envelope already holds a note or it doesn't.

questions.onCorrect: One of them is right already. Not knowing which is a gap in us, not in the envelope. Logic starts there.

choices.label: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.

misconceptions.feedback: Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. It doesn't decide it.
Mia says the note is there and Jon says it isn't. The envelope can't match both.

questions.prompt: A jar holds some sweets and nobody has counted them. How many truth values does “The jar holds an even number of sweets” have right now?
hints: Does the jar hold some number of sweets right now?
Even or odd is already settled by what is in the jar.
In one case, how many verdicts does a claim get?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The jar holds some number, so the claim has already one value, even though no one knows it.

questions.onCorrect: One. The jar's contents settle it, whether or not anyone counts. Not knowing doesn't remove the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Not counting doesn't remove the verdict. The jar already holds some number.
Two verdicts exist, but the contents of the jar have already settled which applies.
“Unknown” describes the counter, not the claim.

questions.prompt: Nobody has opened the envelope. What does that tell us about Mia's claim?
hints: Does opening the envelope change what is inside it?

acceptedIdeas: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has a truth value.

questions.onCorrect: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has its truth value.

choices.label: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
It has no truth value until someone looks.

misconceptions.feedback: Looking finds out what is there. It doesn't put it there.
“Unknown” describes what we know. The claim is checked against the envelope, not against us.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the negation of “The door is open”?
hints: The negation claims that the original fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The door is not open” says the original claim fails.

questions.onCorrect: The negation says the original fails: the door is not open.

misconceptions.feedback: That agrees with the original, with more emphasis. A negation says the original fails.
That asks. It doesn't claim that the original fails.
